Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Islamist fighters in Somalia have made significant gains in the country, according to the latest statement purportedly from al Qaeda's second-in-command, Ayman al-Zawahiri. Ayman al-Zawahiri, pictured here in 2006, also spoke about Yemen, Gaza, Afghanistan and Pakistan. The 25-minute audio recording, titled "From Kabul to Mogadishu," focuses primarily on the "important developments" in Somalia, which al-Zawahiri called "a step on the path of victory of Islam." CNN cannot authenticate the message, which was released on Sunday and was interspersed with television news reports and statements from various al Qaeda-linked commanders. CNN analysts who listened to the recording say the voice is consistent with his intonation and accent. This is the third message from al-Zawahiri espousing the views of the al Qaeda terror network in 2009; the other two focused on Israel's recent military operation against Hamas leaders in Gaza. In addition to Somalia, al-Zawahiri also addresses the situations in Yemen, Gaza, and Afghanistan and Pakistan. Al-Zawahiri praised Al-Shabaab fighters in Somalia who recently seized control of Baidoa, where the U.N.-backed transitional government had been based. He warned the newly installed government, under President Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, not to squander those gains by submitting "to American demands" and not abiding by sharia, or Islamic law. "I call on my Muslim brothers in beloved Somalia ... to not be deceived by those who agree to the secularist constitutions which vie with the sharia in its right to rule," he said. Al-Zawahiri also addressed the "awakening" in Yemen, where many suspected al Qaeda militants wanted in neighboring Saudi Arabia are believed to have fled. That group includes several former detainees of the U.S. military detention facility in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. The al Qaeda leader accused Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Salih and his government of being "servants and slaves" to the United States by allowing Yemen to be used as "a supply center ... against Muslim countries." "How can you agree to let the ruling authority in Yemen be the CIA?" al-Zawahiri asked the people of Yemen. Al-Zawahiri spent the last eight minutes addressing the situation in Afghanistan, Pakistan and Gaza. His focus on Somalia and Yemen -- which accounted for more than 17 minutes of the 25-minute address -- is a departure from the topics of his previous messages. CNN terrorism analyst Peter Bergen suggested that is a reflection of al Qaeda's recent losses as a result of U.S. missile strikes along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. "There were three in 2007 and 34 in 2008 by my count," Bergen said. "These strikes are causing al Qaeda leaders to consider their options." Al Qaeda has considered relocating its base to Somalia or Yemen, according to a former U.S. official who is familiar with the intelligence. Other analysts have suggested that it would be difficult for al Qaeda to gain a stronghold in Somalia because its radical agenda is unpopular in the moderate Islamic country. John Prendergast, who studies the Horn of Africa for the Center for American Progress think tank, said he expects Al-Shabaab's overseas ties to dry up after the recent withdrawal of Ethiopian forces, which was its only basis of support in Somalia. J. Anthony Holmes, director of the Africa program for the Council on Foreign Relations, said it is unlikely Somalia will emerge as "a breeding ground for terrorism" because of its clan-based society. But Bergen noted that both Somalia and Yemen lack a strong central government and "therefore (are) attractive locations for al Qaeda." "Al Qaeda also has had an on-and-off presence in Somalia since 1992 and even earlier in Yemen," he said. "As we have seen also, Yemen's weak government and permissive attitude to jihadists have made it an increasingly attractive venue for Saudi members of al Qaeda." Bergen said that is most likely why al-Zawahiri chose to focus more than half of his latest message on Yemen and Somalia.

(CNN) — Islamist fighters in Somalia have made significant gains across the country, according to the latest statement purportedly issued by al Qaeda’s second-in-command, Ayman al-Zawahiri.

Al-Zawahiri, pictured here in 2006, also discussed Yemen, Gaza, Afghanistan, and Pakistan.

The 25-minute audio recording, titled “From Kabul to Mogadishu,” focuses primarily on what al-Zawahiri described as the “important developments” in Somalia, calling them “a step on the path of victory of Islam.”

CNN cannot authenticate the message, which was released Sunday and interspersed with television news reports and statements from various commanders linked to al Qaeda. CNN analysts who reviewed the recording said the voice is consistent with al-Zawahiri’s intonation and accent.

This is the third message in 2009 from al-Zawahiri espousing the views of the al Qaeda terror network; the previous two focused on Israel’s recent military operation against Hamas leaders in Gaza.

In addition to Somalia, al-Zawahiri addressed the situations in Yemen, Gaza, Afghanistan, and Pakistan.

He praised Al-Shabaab fighters in Somalia who recently seized control of Baidoa, the former base of the U.N.-backed transitional government. He warned the newly installed government, led by President Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, not to squander those gains by submitting “to American demands” or by failing to adhere to sharia, or Islamic law.

“I call on my Muslim brothers in beloved Somalia ... to not be deceived by those who agree to the secularist constitutions which vie with the sharia in its right to rule,” he said.

Al-Zawahiri also addressed the “awakening” in Yemen, where many suspected al Qaeda militants wanted in neighboring Saudi Arabia are believed to have fled. That group includes several former detainees from the U.S. military detention facility at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

The al Qaeda leader accused Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Salih and his government of being “servants and slaves” to the United States by allowing Yemen to be used as “a supply center ... against Muslim countries.”

“How can you agree to let the ruling authority in Yemen be the CIA?” al-Zawahiri asked the people of Yemen.

Al-Zawahiri devoted the final eight minutes of the recording to Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Gaza. His emphasis on Somalia and Yemen—which accounted for more than 17 minutes of the 25-minute address—marks a departure from the focus of his previous messages.

CNN terrorism analyst Peter Bergen suggested the shift reflects al Qaeda’s recent losses as a result of U.S. missile strikes along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.

“There were three in 2007 and 34 in 2008 by my count,” Bergen said. “These strikes are causing al Qaeda leaders to consider their options.”

Al Qaeda has considered relocating its base to Somalia or Yemen, according to a former U.S. official familiar with the intelligence.

Other analysts have suggested that al Qaeda would face difficulty establishing a stronghold in Somalia because its radical agenda is unpopular in the moderate Islamic country.

John Prendergast, who studies the Horn of Africa for the Center for American Progress think tank, said he expects Al-Shabaab’s overseas ties to dry up following the recent withdrawal of Ethiopian forces, which had been its only basis of support in Somalia.

J. Anthony Holmes, director of the Africa program at the Council on Foreign Relations, said it is unlikely Somalia will emerge as “a breeding ground for terrorism” because of its clan-based society.

But Bergen noted that both Somalia and Yemen lack strong central governments and are “therefore attractive locations for al Qaeda.”

“Al Qaeda also has had an on-and-off presence in Somalia since 1992 and even earlier in Yemen,” he said. “As we have seen also, Yemen’s weak government and permissive attitude to jihadists have made it an increasingly attractive venue for Saudi members of al Qaeda.”

Bergen said that is most likely why al-Zawahiri chose to devote more than half of his latest message to Yemen and Somalia.

“Al Qaeda also has had an on-and-off presence in Somalia since 1992 and even earlier in Yemen,” Bergen said. “As we have seen also, Yemen’s weak government and permissive attitude to jihadists have made it an increasingly attractive venue for Saudi members of al Qaeda.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a purported 2009 audio message from Ayman al-Zawahiri titled “From Kabul to Mogadishu,” focusing on al Qaeda’s comments about Somalia, Yemen, Gaza, Afghanistan, and Pakistan.
counterfactuals.output:
**Purported al Qaeda message urges focus on Somalia, Yemen, Gaza, Afghanistan and Pakistan**

A purported audio message from al Qaeda’s then-deputy leader Ayman al-Zawahiri released in 2009 sought to link conflicts across several Muslim-majority regions, invoking Somalia, Yemen, Gaza, Afghanistan and Pakistan as part of the group’s broader narrative against Western-backed governments and U.S. influence.

The message, titled **“From Kabul to Mogadishu,”** was distributed on extremist websites and attributed to Zawahiri, the Egyptian-born militant who was long considered al Qaeda’s chief ideologue and later became its leader after Osama bin Laden’s death. CNN could not independently verify the authenticity of the recording at the time of its purported release.

In the audio, the speaker praised militants in Somalia and framed the country’s conflict as a key front for jihadist movements. Somalia in 2009 was facing severe instability, with the Western-backed transitional government battling Islamist insurgents, including al-Shabaab, which later formally aligned itself with al Qaeda.

The speaker also referred to Yemen, portraying the country as another important arena for militant activity. Around that period, al Qaeda’s Yemen and Saudi branches had merged to form al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, a group that would become one of the network’s most active affiliates.

The message touched on Gaza as well, criticizing Israel and accusing Arab governments of failing Palestinians. Al Qaeda leaders frequently attempted to use the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to broaden their appeal, though Palestinian militant groups such as Hamas have historically had distinct goals, leadership structures and ideological differences from al Qaeda.

On Afghanistan and Pakistan, the speaker urged continued resistance against U.S. and allied forces and criticized Pakistan’s government for cooperating with Washington. At the time, the United States was increasing its focus on both countries, with Afghanistan at the center of the Obama administration’s war strategy and Pakistan under pressure to confront militant sanctuaries in its tribal regions.

Analysts said the message appeared aimed at portraying al Qaeda as relevant across multiple conflicts despite pressure from U.S. counterterrorism operations. By linking Kabul and Mogadishu in the title, the speaker sought to present geographically separate wars as part of a single ideological struggle.

Western intelligence officials have long viewed Zawahiri’s statements as attempts to inspire sympathizers, influence allied militant groups and maintain al Qaeda’s profile amid competition from local insurgencies. The 2009 recording came during a period when al Qaeda’s central leadership was believed to be under pressure in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, even as affiliated groups were gaining visibility in places such as Somalia and Yemen.

**Al-Zawahiri audio message praises Al-Shabaab, weighs in on Yemen; authenticity not confirmed**

An unauthenticated audio recording attributed to al Qaeda leader **Ayman al-Zawahiri** has surfaced online, offering praise for the Somali militant group **Al-Shabaab** and commenting on unrest and jihadist activity in **Yemen**. The message, distributed through jihadist media channels, appears aimed at reinforcing al Qaeda’s relationships with regional affiliates at a time when the organization has increasingly relied on local branches to project influence.

The recording has not been independently verified, and there has been no official confirmation that the voice is al-Zawahiri’s. Analysts noted, however, that the style, themes and distribution method are consistent with previous al Qaeda communications.

### Praise for Al-Shabaab in Somalia

A major focus of the recording is Somalia, where al-Zawahiri praises **Al-Shabaab**, the al Qaeda-aligned militant organization that has fought Somalia’s internationally backed government and African Union forces for years.

In the message, the speaker commends Al-Shabaab’s fighters and frames their campaign as part of a broader global jihadist struggle. The remarks appear intended to strengthen the ideological bond between al Qaeda’s senior leadership and its Somali affiliate, which has been one of the most active and resilient extremist groups in East Africa.

Al-Shabaab formally pledged allegiance to al Qaeda in 2012, but ties between the organizations predated that announcement. The group has carried out attacks inside Somalia and across the region, including in Kenya and Uganda, and has maintained a presence despite military pressure from Somali forces, the African Union mission and U.S. counterterrorism strikes.

Security analysts said the praise is significant because al Qaeda’s central leadership has increasingly depended on regional affiliates — including Al-Shabaab, al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula and groups in North Africa — to maintain relevance after the deaths or arrests of many senior operatives.

### Remarks on Yemen

The recording also addresses **Yemen**, a country that has long been a key theater for al Qaeda activity. The speaker references Yemen’s political turmoil and appears to encourage continued militant resistance there.

Yemen has been home to **al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula**, or AQAP, which U.S. officials have historically considered one of al Qaeda’s most dangerous branches because of its repeated attempts to target Western aviation and its ability to exploit local instability. The country’s fragmented political landscape, tribal dynamics and prolonged conflict have allowed AQAP and other armed groups to survive despite counterterrorism pressure.

The Yemen portion of the message appears designed to link local grievances and instability to al Qaeda’s wider ideological narrative. Analysts said such rhetoric is a recurring feature of al-Zawahiri’s public statements, which often seek to portray regional conflicts as fronts in a single global struggle.

### Peter Bergen: Message shows al Qaeda’s dependence on affiliates

CNN national security analyst **Peter Bergen**, a longtime al Qaeda researcher and author, has argued in similar assessments that al-Zawahiri lacks Osama bin Laden’s charisma and that al Qaeda’s central leadership has been weakened by years of counterterrorism operations. However, Bergen has also emphasized that the organization remains dangerous through its affiliates.

In analysis of messages like this one, Bergen has described al-Zawahiri as an ideological figure who often issues lengthy, doctrinal statements rather than operationally compelling appeals. He has noted that al Qaeda’s center of gravity has shifted away from its original core in Afghanistan and Pakistan toward regional branches in places such as Yemen, Somalia, Syria and North Africa.

Bergen’s broader assessment is that al Qaeda’s central leadership may be diminished, but its franchise model continues to matter. In that context, a message praising Al-Shabaab and addressing Yemen is less about announcing new strategy than about maintaining ideological unity among far-flung militant groups.

### Other experts: A bid for relevance and cohesion

Other terrorism analysts said the recording fits a familiar pattern: al-Zawahiri attempting to position himself as the senior ideological guide for jihadist movements while encouraging affiliates to remain aligned with al Qaeda’s brand.

Experts noted several key themes:

- **Affiliate validation:** By praising Al-Shabaab, al-Zawahiri reinforces the group’s status within al Qaeda’s network and signals approval to supporters.
- **Exploitation of instability:** References to Yemen underscore al Qaeda’s continued focus on failed or fragile states where militants can gain territory, recruits or influence.
- **Propaganda continuity:** Even if al Qaeda’s core is operationally constrained, regular media releases help sustain the perception that its leadership remains active.
- **Competition within jihadist movements:** Messages like this also serve to remind sympathizers that al Qaeda still seeks leadership of the global jihadist cause, particularly after years of competition with ISIS and other factions.

Analysts cautioned that audio statements rarely provide direct evidence of operational capability. Instead, they are best understood as propaganda tools: part morale-building, part ideological messaging and part strategic signaling to followers and affiliates.

### Authentication remains unresolved

As with many recordings attributed to militant leaders, authentication remains a central issue. Governments and intelligence agencies often take time to analyze the voice, production details and distribution pathway before determining whether a message is genuine.

Even if authenticated, experts said the recording does not necessarily indicate an imminent threat. But they added that statements by senior al Qaeda figures can still influence supporters, encourage affiliated groups and shape extremist narratives online.

The recording underscores al Qaeda’s continued effort to bind together regional conflicts — including Somalia and Yemen — under a single ideological framework, even as the group’s central leadership remains under pressure and its operational strength is dispersed among affiliates.

counterfactuals.output:
(CNN) -- Islamist fighters in Somalia have gained ground in recent days, tightening their grip on key areas as the country’s fragile government struggles to contain an insurgency that has drawn increasing attention from al Qaeda’s leadership.

In a 25-minute audio statement released on jihadist websites, al Qaeda’s second-in-command, Ayman al-Zawahiri, praised militants in Somalia and urged Muslims to support fighters there and in Yemen. The authenticity of the recording could not be independently verified, but the voice resembled previous messages attributed to al-Zawahiri.

Al-Zawahiri described Somalia as a critical front in the broader Islamist struggle and called on militants to continue fighting against the Somali government and its backers. He also referred to Yemen, where al Qaeda has sought to expand its influence amid political instability and weak central authority.

Somalia has been mired in conflict for decades, with successive transitional governments unable to assert control over much of the country. Islamist factions have repeatedly battled government forces and African Union peacekeepers, while clan rivalries, famine and lawlessness have deepened the crisis.

The latest advances by Islamist fighters underscore the government’s vulnerability. Officials have warned that militant gains could further destabilize the Horn of Africa and provide a haven for extremist networks with regional and international ambitions.

Western intelligence agencies have long viewed Somalia and Yemen as potential safe havens for al Qaeda-linked groups. Both countries have coastlines along strategic shipping routes, and both have struggled with weak governance, poverty and armed insurgencies.

Al-Zawahiri’s message appeared aimed at linking the conflicts in Somalia and Yemen to al Qaeda’s global narrative, portraying local insurgencies as part of a wider campaign against Western influence and allied governments.

Somali government officials have called for increased international support, including training, funding and military assistance, to counter the Islamist advance. African Union forces have also been deployed in an effort to protect government institutions and prevent militants from taking full control of the capital.

The audio statement comes as al Qaeda continues to rely on recorded messages to communicate with supporters, particularly as pressure from international counterterrorism operations has limited the movement of its senior leaders.

Analysts say the reference to Somalia and Yemen reflects al Qaeda’s continued interest in exploiting instability in failed or weakened states.

“Somalia and Yemen offer the kind of environment extremist groups seek: limited government control, local grievances and access to regional networks,” one security analyst said. “Al-Zawahiri’s comments are intended to encourage those fighters and frame their battles as part of a larger cause.”

The Somali government has vowed to resist the Islamist push, but its forces remain poorly equipped and fragmented. With militants gaining ground and al Qaeda’s leadership publicly highlighting the conflict, concerns are growing that Somalia could become an even more significant front for extremist activity in the region.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the contents and significance of Ayman al-Zawahiri’s 2009 message “From Kabul to Mogadishu,” with background on Al-Shabaab, Yemen-based militants, U.S. missile strikes, and expert views on whether Somalia or Yemen could become al Qaeda bases.
counterfactuals.output:
Ayman al-Zawahiri’s 2009 message **“From Kabul to Mogadishu”** was an al Qaeda propaganda statement that sought to link disparate conflicts—Afghanistan/Pakistan, Somalia, Yemen, and the broader Muslim world—into a single narrative of global jihad. Its title invoked Afghanistan’s capital and Somalia’s capital to suggest that Islamist insurgencies in both places were part of the same struggle against Western-backed governments and U.S. influence.

## Contents of the message

In the message, al-Zawahiri:

- **Praised Somali militants**, especially the insurgents fighting Somalia’s transitional government and African Union forces.
- **Encouraged fighters in Somalia** to continue their campaign and portrayed Somalia as an important front comparable to Afghanistan.
- **Attacked the United States and its allies**, framing U.S. counterterrorism policy, missile strikes, and support for local governments as evidence of a war against Muslims.
- **Linked Somalia with Yemen and Afghanistan/Pakistan**, emphasizing that militant activity across these regions should be seen as interconnected.
- **Called for solidarity among jihadist movements**, urging Muslims to support insurgencies against governments aligned with Washington.

The message was significant less because it announced a new operation than because it reflected al Qaeda central’s effort to **claim ideological leadership** over regional insurgencies and to present local conflicts as components of a global movement.

## Background on Al-Shabaab

At the time, **Al-Shabaab** was Somalia’s most powerful Islamist militant organization. It emerged from the militant wing of the **Islamic Courts Union**, which had briefly controlled much of southern Somalia in 2006 before being ousted by Ethiopian forces backing Somalia’s transitional government.

By 2009, Al-Shabaab controlled substantial territory in southern and central Somalia and was fighting:

- Somalia’s weak Transitional Federal Government,
- Ethiopian-backed or government-aligned forces,
- African Union peacekeepers, especially from Uganda and Burundi.

Al-Shabaab combined Somali nationalist, clan, and Islamist elements, but by this period its leadership was increasingly aligned rhetorically and ideologically with al Qaeda. Foreign fighters had also appeared in Somalia, raising concern among U.S. and regional officials that the country could become a sanctuary for transnational jihadists.

Al-Shabaab did not formally merge with al Qaeda until 2012, but al-Zawahiri’s message was part of the public courtship and mutual reinforcement between the two movements.

## Yemen-based militants

Yemen was also becoming a major concern in 2009. Militants there had reorganized under the banner of **al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula**, or **AQAP**, formed from Saudi and Yemeni jihadist networks. Yemen’s weak central government, mountainous terrain, tribal politics, and history of militant activity made it attractive to al Qaeda-linked figures.

AQAP was viewed by many analysts as especially dangerous because it combined:

- experienced militants,
- access to regional networks,
- a permissive security environment,
- proximity to Saudi Arabia and key maritime routes.

Al-Zawahiri’s references to Yemen fit al Qaeda’s broader effort to elevate Yemen as a central arena after pressure on al Qaeda’s core leadership in Pakistan.

## U.S. missile strikes and counterterrorism pressure

The message also came amid intensified U.S. counterterrorism operations, especially missile and drone strikes against al Qaeda and affiliated militants in Pakistan’s tribal areas, and occasional strikes or raids targeting militants elsewhere.

Al-Zawahiri used these strikes rhetorically, portraying them as indiscriminate aggression and using civilian casualties or sovereignty concerns to bolster recruitment narratives. From the U.S. perspective, such strikes were intended to disrupt al Qaeda leadership and prevent safe havens from forming. But critics argued that they could also fuel anti-American sentiment and strengthen militant propaganda.

In Somalia and Yemen, the central policy concern was whether weak states could become alternatives to Pakistan/Afghanistan as operational bases for al Qaeda-linked groups.

## Could Somalia or Yemen become al Qaeda bases?

Experts at the time were divided, but many saw both countries as serious risks.

### Somalia

Some analysts warned that Somalia’s lawlessness, weak government, coastline, and active insurgency made it a potential al Qaeda haven. Al-Shabaab’s growing ideological affinity with al Qaeda and presence of foreign fighters reinforced that concern.

Others cautioned against overstating the threat. They argued that Somalia’s clan dynamics, local grievances, and Al-Shabaab’s domestic priorities limited al Qaeda central’s ability to use Somalia as a command-and-control hub. Somalia was dangerous, but not necessarily another Afghanistan.

### Yemen

Yemen was often seen as the more plausible base for transnational plotting. AQAP had deep local roots, and Yemen’s geography and political fragmentation gave militants room to operate. Analysts worried that Yemen-based militants could target Western interests, Saudi Arabia, or international aviation and shipping.

Still, experts also noted constraints: Yemeni tribal politics were complex, the government retained some counterterrorism capacity, and AQAP’s ambitions could provoke local resistance.

## Significance

“From Kabul to Mogadishu” showed al Qaeda trying to adapt to pressure on its core leadership by promoting a **decentralized jihadist network**. Rather than relying solely on Afghanistan and Pakistan, al-Zawahiri highlighted Somalia and Yemen as emerging fronts.

The message mattered because it:

- elevated Al-Shabaab’s importance in al Qaeda propaganda,
- underscored Yemen’s growing role in jihadist strategy,
- reflected al Qaeda’s shift toward affiliates and regional franchises,
- highlighted the challenge weak states posed for counterterrorism,
- foreshadowed later concerns about AQAP and Al-Shabaab as durable al Qaeda-aligned organizations.

In short, the statement was both propaganda and strategic messaging: al-Zawahiri was attempting to bind local insurgencies into al Qaeda’s global brand while encouraging supporters to see Somalia and Yemen as successors or complements to Afghanistan as arenas of jihadist struggle.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a full-length wire-service style report on an audio message attributed to Ayman al-Zawahiri, noting CNN cannot authenticate it, quoting his warnings to Somalia and Yemen, and explaining why analysts think al Qaeda may be shifting attention away from Afghanistan and Pakistan.
counterfactuals.output:
**Audio attributed to al Qaeda’s al-Zawahiri warns Somalia, Yemen; analysts see shift in focus**

An audio message attributed to al Qaeda’s No. 2 leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri, warned militants in Somalia and Yemen to prepare for confrontation with the United States and its allies, in what analysts said may reflect the network’s growing emphasis on unstable states outside its traditional Afghanistan-Pakistan base.

CNN could not independently authenticate the recording. The voice on the message was said to be Zawahiri’s, and the recording was distributed on militant websites, according to groups that monitor extremist media.

In the message, the speaker addressed Somalia and Yemen directly, portraying both as emerging fronts in al Qaeda’s conflict with the West and regional governments.

To Somalia, the speaker warned that foreign-backed forces would try to reverse militant gains and urged Islamist fighters there not to compromise.

“Beware of the conspiracies being plotted against you,” the voice said in remarks directed at Somalia, according to a translation of the message. “Stand firm, be patient and do not lay down your weapons.”

The speaker also referred to Yemen as a crucial battleground and accused its government of acting on behalf of Washington.

“To the people of Yemen, beware: America and its agents are preparing to strike you,” the voice said. “Do not allow Yemen to become a base for the Crusaders and their collaborators.”

The recording did not contain a direct claim of responsibility for a specific attack. Instead, it appeared to be a strategic message aimed at encouraging al Qaeda-linked movements and supporters in countries where central governments have struggled to maintain authority.

Analysts said the emphasis on Somalia and Yemen is notable because it comes as al Qaeda’s core leadership has been under sustained pressure in Afghanistan and Pakistan. U.S. drone strikes, Pakistani military operations and intelligence campaigns have made it harder for senior al Qaeda figures to communicate, train recruits and plan attacks from the tribal areas along the Afghan-Pakistani border.

At the same time, al Qaeda’s regional affiliates and ideological allies have become more prominent.

In Yemen, al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, or AQAP, has taken advantage of weak governance, tribal grievances and rugged terrain to build one of the network’s most active branches. U.S. officials have long viewed AQAP as a serious threat because of its interest in attacking Western targets and its ability to recruit beyond Yemen.

In Somalia, al-Shabaab, an Islamist militant group with ties to al Qaeda, has fought the Somali government and African Union forces for years. The country’s prolonged instability has made it a recurring concern for counterterrorism officials, who fear it could provide space for training camps, foreign fighters and attacks in the region.

Analysts said Zawahiri’s message may be an attempt to reinforce al Qaeda’s relevance by aligning the central leadership with conflicts where local militants have momentum. Rather than relying solely on Afghanistan and Pakistan, al Qaeda has increasingly promoted a decentralized model in which affiliates carry out attacks, control territory or spread propaganda under the broader al Qaeda banner.

The shift also reflects opportunity. Yemen and Somalia offer conditions al Qaeda has historically exploited: weak state institutions, local conflicts, anti-government sentiment and limited security control in remote areas. By highlighting those countries, the speaker appeared to be encouraging supporters to view them as priority fronts.

Counterterrorism specialists cautioned, however, that a propaganda message does not necessarily mean al Qaeda’s central command is directing operations in either country. The network often seeks to claim ideological leadership over local insurgencies, even when operational links are loose.

Still, the recording underscores the continuing importance of al Qaeda’s media strategy. Even as its senior leaders face pressure, the group has used audio and video messages to project influence, rally supporters and frame local conflicts as part of a global campaign.

Zawahiri, an Egyptian physician who became Osama bin Laden’s deputy, has long served as one of al Qaeda’s chief ideologues and public voices. Messages attributed to him have frequently called for attacks on the United States and its allies while urging militants in regional conflicts to adopt al Qaeda’s global agenda.

U.S. and allied intelligence officials typically review such recordings for clues about timing, location, leadership status and strategic priorities. But authentication can be difficult, especially when messages are released through online extremist channels rather than directly by an identifiable source.

The latest message, if genuine, suggests that al Qaeda’s leadership is continuing to look beyond Afghanistan and Pakistan, placing greater rhetorical and strategic weight on countries where affiliated groups can operate with fewer constraints.
